unitDescription.value: In this unit, students will explore how websites and servers work by interacting with a controlled, deliberately vulnerable web application. Through guided investigation and hands-on challenges, students will examine how data moves between a browser and server, how user input is processed, and how poor design choices can create security weaknesses. Students will test, identify and explain simple vulnerabilities in a safe learning environment, then recommend and apply improvements to make the system more secure. This unit develops practical understanding of web technologies, ethical hacking, secure design principles and responsible digital behaviour.

cohortAndClassConsiderations.value: The Years 9–10 cohort consists of a diverse group of boys with a wide range of digital competencies, from students with strong technical skills and personal interest in IT, to those who require further support to confidently engage with digital systems. Many students come from regional or rural backgrounds, where access to structured digital learning opportunities may have been limited. The program is designed to build on prior knowledge while introducing more advanced and applied skills relevant to future study and employment. The curriculum supports the school’s priority to equip students with transferable digital skills, critical thinking abilities, and an understanding of ethical technology use in a rapidly changing world.

description.value: Students will complete a written examination to assess their understanding of the interdependencies between hardware and software components within networked digital systems, with a focus on mechanisms for managing, controlling, and securing data access. The assessment requires students to explain the abstraction of online documents by distinguishing between content, structure, and presentation, and to justify the importance of these representations in contemporary web environments.

conditions.value: Up to 50 minutes plus 10 minutes planning time; under supervised conditions; short response up to 100 words per item, up to 600 words for the task; extended response 200–300 words per item, up to 600 words for the task

achievementStandard.value: By the end of Year 10 students develop and modify innovative digital solutions, decompose real-world problems, and critically evaluate alternative solutions against stakeholder elicited user stories. Students acquire, interpret and model complex data with databases and represent documents as content, structure and presentation. They design and validate algorithms and implement them, including in an object-oriented programming language. Students explain how digital systems manage, control and secure access to data; and model cyber security threats and explore a vulnerability. They use advanced features of digital tools to create interactive content, and to plan, collaborate on, and manage agile projects. Students apply privacy principles to manage digital footprints.

moderation.value: A sample of student portfolios representing a range of achievement levels will be reviewed by another Digital Technologies teacher.

description.value: Students investigate the architecture of networked digital systems, focusing on how hardware and software components manage, control, and secure access to data. Through the analysis of a provided web application, students identify software vulnerabilities and apply their knowledge of content, structure, and presentation to propose and implement robust, secure, and user-friendly modifications. The task requires students to develop a cyber security threat model, critique the system’s digital footprint against the Australian Privacy Principles, and employ object-oriented programming to debug and harden server-side logic and input validation. Students document the problem-solving process, justifying their design choices against established criteria, user stories, and potential future enterprise impacts. The final solution is evaluated for its effectiveness in mitigating identified risks and improving overall system integrity.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Focus on the client-server relationship and how requests are processed across a network. Students engage in discussions regarding the physical and logical components that enable web connectivity.

resources.value: Web browser developer tools, classroom demonstration of packet tracing, online simulations of the client-server model, introductory worksheet on network infrastructure.

theory.value: Students investigate how the internet functions as a network of digital systems, focusing on the roles of hardware (servers, routers, client devices) and software (browsers, web servers) in managing and transmitting data. Key terminology such as client-server model, IP address, and DNS is introduced. Students develop an understanding of how data is requested, transferred, and displayed in a web context.

lessons.title: Foundations of the Internet: Client-Server Architecture
lessons.learningGoal: Explain the role of the client-server model in the transmission of data across a network.

orientate.smartStart: Students complete a quick-write: 'In one sentence, describe what happens when you type a web address into your browser and press Enter.'
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can explain how a browser (client) asks for and receives information from a web server

activities.title: Core Network Vocabulary
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the client-server relationship using the restaurant analogy: the Client acts as the customer placing an order, and the Server acts as the waiter fulfilling that request. Model the definition writing process: emphasize clarity, precision, and the relationship between terminology and system function. Provide the example: 'Client: A hardware device or software program that initiates a communication session to request resources.'
activities.studentsDo: Complete the 'DEFINE n terms' table by matching the provided definitions to the correct core network terminology using the glossary resource provided.
activities.visibleInstructions: Use the provided glossary to complete the definitions table. Ensure your definitions focus on the functional role of each component within the network.
activities.questioning:
question: If the client is the customer, what does the 'request' represent in the restaurant analogy?
expectedAnswer: The request represents the order placed by the customer, equivalent to an HTTP request for specific data.
question: What happens if the 'server' is offline?
expectedAnswer: The communication cycle is broken; the client cannot receive the requested resources, resulting in a 'connection error' or timeout.
activities.scaffolding: Client: The device or browser application that initiates a communication session to request resources. Server: A remote computer system that stores web files and delivers them to clients upon request. Request: A message sent from a client to a server asking for data (e.g., an HTML file or image). Response: The data packet(s) returned from the server to the client after processing the request.
activities.eLearning: Students access the school intranet glossary portal to verify technical definitions.
activities.transition: Transition students by asking them to identify one real-world server they interact with daily before moving to the simulation phase.
activities.teacherAnswerKey: Client: The device or software that requests data. Server: The system that hosts resources and processes client requests. Request: An instruction sent from the client to the server for specific information. Response: The data transmitted by the server back to the client completing the cycle.

activities.title: The Request-Response Cycle
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly model the lifecycle of an HTTP request. Draw the client-server interaction on the board: User Input (Browser) -> Request (HTTP) -> Server Processing -> Response (Data) -> Rendering. Use the example of a student visiting the St Brendan's College website to clarify: 'The browser (client) asks the St Brendan's College web server for the homepage data, and the server returns exactly what is needed for your screen to render the page.'
activities.studentsDo: Complete the cloze passage to consolidate understanding of network communication protocols.
activities.visibleInstructions: Use the word bank to complete the sentences describing the client-server architecture. Ensure your terminology is precise.
activities.questioning:
question: Why does data require a distinct 'request' and 'response' rather than being continuously pushed to the client?
expectedAnswer: It manages network bandwidth efficiency; the server only transmits the specific data requested, preventing network congestion and reducing latency.
question: What happens if a client requests a URL that does not exist on the server?
expectedAnswer: The server processes the request, identifies that the resource is missing, and returns an error status code, typically a 404 Not Found, rather than the requested page data.
activities.scaffolding:
Client-Server Relationship: 
1. Client: The software/hardware requesting resources (e.g., Chrome, Firefox). 
2. Server: The powerful computer that hosts and delivers resources. 
3. HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol): The set of rules defining how messages are formatted and transmitted. 
4. Packet: Small units of data used to transport information across the internet.
activities.eLearning: Students may use their browser's 'Network' tab in Developer Tools to observe the request-response cycle in action when loading the St Brendan's College homepage.
activities.transition: Transition to diagramming the packet path across a wide area network.

workbookSpec.title: The Mechanics of HTTP Communication
workbookSpec.prompt: Complete the summary below regarding the interaction between client devices and web servers.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: 1: URL, 2: browser, 3: request, 4: response, 5: packet, 6: HTTP
workbookSpec.text: When a user inputs a {{1}} into their web {{2}}, the device initiates an HTTP {{3}} to the destination server. The server retrieves the relevant files and sends an HTTP {{4}} containing the content back to the client. During this transmission, the data is broken down into a small {{5}} to ensure it travels across the network efficiently. This process is governed by the {{6}} protocol, which ensures consistency in data exchange.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: 1. URL (Uniform Resource Locator); 2. browser (Client software); 3. request (Client-sent message); 4. response (Server-sent message); 5. packet (Data transfer unit); 6. HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol).

activities.title: Mapping the Request Flow
activities.teacherDoes: Model the request-response cycle using the St Brendan's College website domain as the primary example. Explicitly demonstrate that 'Request' flows outbound (Client to Server) and 'Response' flows inbound (Server to Client). Use the analogy of a letter service: the address is the IP/URL, and the mail is the data packet. Scaffolding example on board: [User Clicks Link] -> [Browser resolves IP via DNS] -> [GET Request sent] -> [Server processes] -> [HTML/CSS delivered].
activities.studentsDo: Complete the data flow diagram in the workbook to map the lifecycle of a single HTTP request for a page on the St Brendan's College website.
activities.visibleInstructions: Trace the path of a request from your device to the St Brendan's College web server. Number each stage in the flowchart clearly. Ensure you account for both the request (outbound) and the response (inbound).
activities.questioning:
question: What happens if the web server at the destination address is offline when the request arrives?
expected: The client receives an error code (e.g., 404 or 503) because the request-response cycle cannot be completed.
question: How does the 'Internet' node in your diagram manage to route data to the correct specific server instead of all servers globally?
expected: The Internet uses IP addressing and routing protocols to direct packets to the unique IP address associated with the domain name.
activities.scaffolding: Request Lifecycle: 1. User Input (URL) -> 2. DNS Resolution (Finding the Server) -> 3. TCP Handshake -> 4. HTTP Request (GET) -> 5. Server Processing -> 6. Data Packet Delivery -> 7. Browser Rendering.
activities.eLearning: Monitor student understanding of the two-way transmission. If students struggle, ensure they distinguish between the 'Client' (browser) and the 'Server' (remote host). Use the browser's 'Network' tab in Developer Tools if available as a real-time verification.
activities.transition: Conclude the session by summarising how these discrete packets form the foundation of 'loading' a page, setting the scene for next lesson's discussion on web protocols.

workbookSpec.title: The Web Request Cycle
workbookSpec.prompt: Complete the flow chart representing the journey of a data request from your browser to the St Brendan's College server.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: 1. User initiates URL request -> 2. DNS translates domain to IP address -> 3. Request travels via Router to Internet -> 4. Server receives GET request -> 5. Server validates request -> 6. Data packets return via Internet -> 7. Browser renders website.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Step 1: User types stbrendans.qld.edu.au; Step 2: DNS maps to Server IP; Step 3: Request leaves local gateway; Step 4: Packets route across ISP infrastructure; Step 5: Web Server identifies requested HTML file; Step 6: Data packets traverse back through the internet to the client browser. Yes path leads to page load, No path leads to error handling.

culminate.smartFinish: 3-2-1 Exit Ticket: Write 3 things you learned about web requests, 2 questions you still have, and 1 analogy for how servers work.
culminate.summarise: Recap the client-server relationship and how requests enable us to view web content.
culminate.nextSteps: Tomorrow we will use developer tools to see this 'request' happening in real-time.

lessons.resources: Whiteboard, Workbook, Access to St Brendan's College website.

lessons.title: Inspecting the Web: Browser Developer Tools
lessons.learningGoal: Use browser developer tools to inspect the network requests made when loading a website.

orientate.smartStart: Quick review: What is the primary difference between the Client and the Server?
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can use Network inspection tools to view how data is transferred between a browser and a server

activities.title: I Do: Inspecting Network Activity
activities.teacherDoes: Project the St Brendan's College homepage. Open Chrome Developer Tools (F12 or Ctrl+Shift+I) and navigate to the Network tab. Demonstrate: 1. Disabling cache to ensure fresh requests. 2. Reloading the page. 3. Identifying the waterfall chart and request list. Say: 'Notice that a single URL, such as our college homepage, is actually a collection of dozens of distinct resources. The server does not send one giant file; it sends a skeleton HTML file, which then tells your browser to fetch style sheets, scripts, and high-resolution images individually.' Model how to hover over a request to see the full URL path, emphasizing the client-server relationship for each line item.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher model the request-response lifecycle. Follow along by opening Developer Tools on their local machines, focusing on the 'Name' and 'Status' columns to observe live network traffic.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the Network tab as the page reloads. Watch the waterfall chart build the page structure line by line. Notice how each 'Status 200 OK' confirms that the client successfully requested and received a piece of the website.
activities.questioning:
question: Why are there so many lines in the Network tab when I only requested one URL?
expected: A modern webpage is modular; the browser must send separate, individual requests for every image, script, stylesheet, and font file required to construct the visual page.
question: What does a 'Status 200 OK' tell us about the communication between client and server?
expected: It indicates a successful request-response cycle where the server found the requested resource and sent it to the client without error.
activities.scaffolding:
Key Columns: Name: The filename or resource identifier requested by the browser.
Status: The HTTP status code. 200 means success; 404 means not found; 500 means server error.
Type: The file format (e.g., document, stylesheet, image, script).
Waterfall: The visual representation of how long each request took to load and process.
Definitions: Client: The browser requesting resources.
Server: The computer storing the files and responding to requests.
activities.eLearning: Use the projector for live demonstration. Ensure students have their browser Developer Tools open and docked to the bottom or right side.
activities.transition: Transition to guided student investigation of other local websites.

workbookSpec.title: Anatomy of a Web Request
workbookSpec.prompt: Identify the critical components of the Network Tab interface as demonstrated. Annotate the screenshot below using the numbered legend provided.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: 1: Request Name (The specific asset being fetched), 2: Status Column (HTTP 200 indicates success), 3: Type (File format identifying content), 4: Waterfall (Visual timeline of the transfer speed).
workbookSpec.figureHint: A high-resolution screenshot of a Chrome Network Tab showing a list of requests, including images, CSS files, and JS files with Status 200.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: 1. Request Name: The URI or specific file path being retrieved. 2. Status: Confirms successful communication (200) or error states (404/500). 3. Type: Distinguishes between document, stylesheet, image, or script content. 4. Waterfall: Represents the timing of the request, showing latency and download duration.

activities.title: We Do: Investigating Local Sites
activities.teacherDoes: Direct students to access the Keppel Bay Marina website. Model the use of the F12 developer tools, specifically the Network tab, to observe the request-response cycle. Explain the significance of HTTP 200 (Success) versus other codes. Model: 'I am filtering for 'Img' to see which assets are being requested by the server.'
activities.studentsDo: Navigate to the designated website on local devices. Use the Network tab to monitor incoming traffic. Refresh the page to capture the full request list and classify the types of files transmitted from the server to the client browser.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Navigate to https://www.keppelbaymarina.com.au/. 2. Open Developer Tools (F12) and select the 'Network' tab. 3. Refresh the page (Ctrl + R). 4. Use the table below to classify the request types you observe in the log.
activities.questioning:
question: What is the function of the HTTP 200 status code within the request log?
expected: It indicates that the client request was successfully received, understood, and accepted by the server.
question: Why might a browser choose not to request every single image file again upon refreshing the page?
expected: The browser uses caching to store previously downloaded files locally, reducing redundant network requests and speeding up load times.
activities.scaffolding:
Request Types: 
- Document: The base HTML file that structures the webpage content.
- Stylesheet: Files (CSS) that dictate the visual presentation and layout.
- Script: Files (JavaScript) that enable dynamic or interactive page elements.
- Image: Media files (JPG, PNG, SVG) displayed on the page.
activities.eLearning: Monitor device connectivity. Ensure students are looking at the 'Network' sub-tab rather than 'Console' or 'Elements'. Assist students in enabling 'Disable cache' in the Network tab to ensure they see fresh requests.
activities.transition: Transition students to independent activity by asking them to compare their request list with a partner's screen.
activities.workbookMaterials: Network Inspection Table for Keppel Bay Marina audit.
activities.teacherAnswerKey: Expected Results: Document should always be 200. Stylesheets and Scripts are usually 200 unless cached (then 304). Images are usually 200. Students should tick all rows provided they have loaded the page correctly.

activities.title: You Do: Documenting Findings
activities.teacherDoes: Distribute the workbook pages. Direct students to inspect the St Brendan's College website using the 'Network' tab. Model how to locate the 'Status' column for the primary document request. Explain that '200' is the standard success code, while others indicate specific server communication issues. Circulate to check that students can differentiate between successful resource loading and errors.
activities.studentsDo: Navigate to the St Brendan's College website. Open Browser Developer Tools (F12), refresh the page, and select the 'Network' tab. Identify the status codes for the initial GET request and record findings in the workbook, justifying why these codes are critical for maintenance.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. Inspect the St Brendan's College website network activity.
2. Locate the primary document request and its status code.
3. Complete the reflection identifying why developers must monitor these status codes.
activities.questioning:
question: Why does a 200 status code provide assurance regarding the integrity of the client-server connection?
expected: A 200 OK status indicates that the server received the client's request, processed it, and successfully returned the requested resource.
question: How might a web developer use status codes like 404 or 500 to troubleshoot a broken webpage?
expected: These codes signal specific failures—404 identifies a missing resource (client-side link error), while 500 identifies a server-side execution error, allowing for targeted debugging.
activities.scaffolding:
Status Codes Reference:
- 200 (OK): Request succeeded.
- 301/302 (Redirect): Resource moved.
- 404 (Not Found): Resource does not exist.
- 500 (Internal Server Error): Server encountered an unexpected condition.
activities.eLearning: Browser Developer Tools (F12) enabled in Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge.
activities.transition: Close Developer Tools and save the workbook page for submission.

workbookSpec.title: Network Analysis Reflection
workbookSpec.prompt: Document your analysis of the web request cycle.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Expected answer: A status code is crucial because it acts as a diagnostic signal for the communication health between the client browser and the web server. A '200 OK' confirms successful transmission, whereas error codes (4xx or 5xx) allow developers to distinguish between issues caused by incorrect client-side paths or server-side crashes, directly informing the remediation process.

culminate.smartFinish: Show of hands: Who found a file that failed to load (Status 404)?
culminate.summarise: We successfully used browser tools to 'see' the invisible client-server dialogue.
culminate.nextSteps: Next lesson we explore the infrastructure (DNS, IP) that makes this routing possible.

lessons.resources: Web browsers, Keppel Bay Marina website.

lessons.title: Network Infrastructure: How the Internet Connects
lessons.learningGoal: Identify the key infrastructure components (IP, DNS, Router) that enable web communication.

orientate.smartStart: Spaced retrieval: Briefly explain the difference between a Client and a Server using one key term from last lesson.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can identify the function of IP addresses and DNS in directing web traffic

activities.title: Hardware & Protocol Match
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly model the client-server interaction by describing a user request: 'When you type a URL, your browser needs the server address.' Introduce DNS as the directory service (phonebook) and IP Address as the specific device location. Use the whiteboard to diagram a data packet travelling through a router, defining it as the traffic controller that determines the most efficient path between sub-networks.
activities.studentsDo: Students correlate technical infrastructure terms with their functional definitions to build understanding of the request-response cycle. They complete the matching table provided in the workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: Using the provided definition bank, match each infrastructure component to its correct description in the table below.
activities.questioning:
question: If DNS is the 'phonebook' of the internet, what information does it retrieve for the client?
expectedAnswer: It retrieves the corresponding IP address for a human-readable domain name (e.g., google.com).
question: In the context of network infrastructure, why is a router essential when connecting a local network to the internet?
expectedAnswer: A router acts as a gateway or traffic controller, directing data packets between different network segments and managing the flow of traffic.
activities.scaffolding: DNS (Domain Name System): A decentralised naming system that maps human-readable hostnames to IP addresses. IP Address: A unique numerical identifier assigned to each device connected to a computer network. Router: A networking device that forwards data packets between computer networks.
activities.eLearning: Students access the 'St Brendan's College' website via the browser to verify their IP connection during the practical demonstration.
activities.transition: Transition students to the packet-tracing simulation to observe these components in active communication.

workbookSpec.title: Infrastructure Functionality Match
workbookSpec.prompt: Match the infrastructure component to the correct definition provided in the bank.
bank: A: The numeric label assigned to a device on a network.
B: Hardware device that forwards data packets between networks.
C: System that translates domain names into IP addresses.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: DNS: C; IP Address: A; Router: B.

activities.title: How DNS Works
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the Domain Name System (DNS) as the phonebook of the internet. Model the request process: 'When you type www.stbrendans.qld.edu.au, your browser doesn't know where that is. It queries a DNS server to translate the friendly name into the specific server IP address.' Demonstrate how a typo in a DNS record makes a site 'unreachable' to emphasize the system's precision.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the guided cloze notes to establish foundational knowledge of network address translation.
activities.visibleInstructions: Read the text carefully and select the appropriate term from the word bank to complete the DNS resolution process description.
activities.questioning:
question: If the DNS server is down, what happens when you try to load a website?
expected: The browser cannot resolve the domain name to an IP address, so the site will fail to load even if the server is active.
question: Why is it inefficient for every computer on the internet to store its own copy of the entire DNS database?
expected: The internet is too large and changes too quickly; centralized or hierarchical DNS servers ensure updates are managed efficiently and data remains consistent.
activities.scaffolding: DNS Process Overview: 1. User inputs URL. 2. Resolver checks for IP address. 3. If missing, it queries a Root Server -> TLD Server -> Authoritative Name Server. 4. IP address is returned to the user device. 5. Browser requests data from the IP address.
activities.eLearning: None.
activities.transition: Proceed to activity 3: Packet Tracing and Simulation.

workbookSpec.title: DNS Resolution Process
workbookSpec.prompt: Complete the sentences to define the role of the Domain Name System.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: 1. DNS, 2. IP address, 3. recursive resolver, 4. clients
workbookSpec.text: The {{1}} acts as a critical link in web infrastructure, functioning essentially as the phonebook of the internet. Because human-readable addresses like 'stbrendans.qld.edu.au' are difficult for machines to route, the system translates them into a unique {{2}}. This request is handled by a {{3}}, which manages the directory of records. Without this automated mapping, internet traffic would struggle to navigate between {{4}} and servers.

activities.workbookMaterials: DNS Concept Notes and Resolution Flowchart
activities.teacherAnswerKey: 1. DNS (The Domain Name System). 2. IP address (The specific numeric address required for routing). 3. recursive resolver (The server that performs the lookups). 4. clients (The user devices requesting the information).

activities.title: Mapping the Internet Infrastructure
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the pathway of a request-response cycle. Explain the 'Handshake' concept: 1. Client (Browser) sends Request; 2. DNS resolves the IP; 3. Server receives request; 4. Data packets return via Router. Model by drawing an example packet flow on the whiteboard, highlighting how the router directs traffic.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the 'Infrastructure Flow' diagram by labelling nodes and drawing the communication path between the user device and the remote web server, indicating the role of the DNS server as the 'directory'.
activities.visibleInstructions: Label the five infrastructure components: Device, Local Router, ISP (Internet Service Provider), DNS Server, and Web Server. Draw arrows to trace the path a request takes when visiting www.stbrendans.qld.edu.au.
activities.questioning:
question: What happens if the DNS server is unreachable but you already have the IP address cached?
expected: The client can still connect directly to the Web Server using the IP address without needing the DNS directory service.
question: Why does a router need to be 'smart' about traffic?
expected: It must determine the most efficient path for data packets to traverse across complex interconnected networks to avoid congestion.
activities.scaffolding:
Infrastructure Definition Key:
- Device: The user hardware requesting content.
- Router: The gateway device connecting the local network to the ISP.
- ISP: The telecommunications company providing the internet connection.
- DNS Server: The 'phonebook' of the internet that translates domain names to IP addresses.
- Web Server: The host machine storing the website files.
activities.eLearning: None.
activities.transition: Transition to independent review of web structure using browser developer tools.

workbookSpec.title: Internet Infrastructure Flow Diagram
workbookSpec.prompt: Using the definitions provided, label the five infrastructure components below. Connect them with arrows indicating the request pathway for a browser navigation event.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Client -> Router -> ISP -> (Query) -> DNS Server -> (Return IP) -> ISP -> Web Server (Request Content) -> ISP -> Router -> Client (Render Page).

activities.teacherAnswerKey: The correct diagram flow starts at the 'Device' node, connecting to the 'Router'. The path branches to the 'DNS Server' for resolution, then proceeds through the 'ISP' to the 'Web Server'. The return path traces back through the same infrastructure nodes. Ensure students label: 1. Device (User), 2. Local Router (Gateway), 3. ISP (Transit), 4. DNS Server (Resolution), 5. Web Server (Destination).

culminate.smartFinish: 3-2-1 exit ticket: 3 network components, 2 reasons why DNS matters, 1 question about next week.
culminate.summarise: We have covered the physical (routers, cables) and logical (IPs, DNS) infrastructure of the internet.
culminate.nextSteps: Next week we move to structuring web content with HTML.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Emphasis on the separation of content from presentation through the study of HTML semantic elements. Students begin to understand the hierarchical nature of document structure.

resources.value: Code editor (e.g., VS Code or similar), HTML starter templates, W3Schools documentation, browser live-preview tools.

theory.value: Students are introduced to how web content is structured using HTML. The concept of representing information as content and structure is explicitly taught. Students learn about common HTML elements (headings, paragraphs, images, links) and the purpose of semantic structure.

prac.value: Students begin writing basic HTML documents using a code editor. They create a simple webpage including headings, paragraphs, and images. Emphasis is placed on correct syntax, file structure, and readability of code.

workbookSpec.text: Every valid HTML document must start with the {{1}} declaration to inform the browser of the document type. The entire document is then wrapped within the {{2}} element, which acts as the root. Information that does not appear directly on the webpage, such as the page title and internal styles, is classified as {{3}} and placed within the {{4}} section. Conversely, all content that the user interacts with—including headings, images, and text—resides within the {{5}} tag.

activities.title: Analyzing Web Structure
activities.teacherDoes: Explain that professional web design separates structural elements from styling. Direct students to the St Brendan's College website. Model identifying a structural 'Header' block (navigation and logo), the 'Main' content area (body copy and images), and the 'Footer' block (links and legal disclaimers). Demonstrate how identifying these regions helps in planning semantic HTML code structure.

activities.visibleInstructions: Navigate to the St Brendan's College website. Identify the three primary structural regions (Header, Main, Footer). Describe the specific content found within each section and explain its function for the user experience.
activities.questioning:
question: Why do web developers standardise the layout of the Header and Footer across a multi-page website?
expected: Consistency allows users to intuitively navigate and find information (e.g., contact details or navigation menus) regardless of which page they are currently viewing.
question: What might happen to a user's experience if the 'Main' content area lacked a clear visual distinction from the Header?
expected: The user would likely find the content difficult to scan, leading to confusion about which elements are navigational tools and which are the primary information they came to read.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions: 
1. Header: The top section of a website usually containing the logo and primary navigation links.
2. Main: The central section of a webpage that holds the unique, primary content relevant to the specific page.
3. Footer: The bottom section of a website, typically containing supplementary information, copyright details, and secondary navigation.

activities.transition: Conclude by summarising how these three areas translate directly into the HTML5 semantic tags: <header>, <main>, and <footer>.

activities.title: CSS Vocabulary
activities.teacherDoes: Explain that CSS acts as the 'style sheet' for a document, allowing for a clean Separation of Concerns. Model the syntax anatomy on the board: p { color: red; }. Emphasize that p is the Selector, color is the Property, and red is the Value. Together, color: red; forms a Declaration.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the 'CSS Terminology Match' table by selecting the correct definition from the bank for each term.
activities.visibleInstructions: Using the provided bank of definitions, write the correct definition letter or phrase in the Match column for each CSS term.
activities.questioning:
question: If I want to target all h1 tags to change their appearance, which part of the CSS rule do I change?
expectedAnswer: The Selector (specifically, changing it to h1).
question: Why is it considered best practice to use external CSS rather than inline styles?
expectedAnswer: It enforces the 'Separation of Concerns' principle, making the site easier to maintain, faster to update globally, and cleaner to read.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions: 
Selector: Identifies the HTML element to be styled.
Property: The specific design attribute to modify (e.g., colour, font-size).
Value: The specific setting applied to the property (e.g., #0000FF, 16px).
Declaration: The combination of property and value (e.g., color: blue;).
activities.eLearning: Display the CSS syntax diagram on the main projector, highlighting the syntax: Selector { Property: Value; }.

The complete pair of property and value (e.g., color: blue;)

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Selector: The specific HTML element being targeted (e.g., h1, p). Property: The specific design attribute to change (e.g., color, font-size). Value: The setting applied to the attribute (e.g., blue, 16px). Declaration: The complete pair of property and value (e.g., color: blue;).

activities.title: HTML vs CSS Roles
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the 'Separation of Concerns' principle. Use a standard text editor to show an HTML file and its raw appearance in a browser, then introduce a linked CSS file to style it. Explain that HTML defines the semantic 'skeleton' of the document, while CSS acts as the 'skin' or presentation layer. Model the process: 'When I want to change the font size of all headings, I do not edit each HTML tag; instead, I define a single CSS rule.'
activities.studentsDo: Follow along with the teacher's demonstration, observe the transformation of the raw HTML into a styled page, and complete the guided notes in their workbooks to solidify the conceptual distinction.
activities.visibleInstructions: Use the word bank to complete the sentences describing the relationship between HTML structure and CSS presentation.
activities.questioning:
question: If you wanted to change the colour of every paragraph on a 50-page website, why is CSS more efficient than modifying HTML tags?
expectedAnswer: CSS allows for a single update in an external stylesheet that propagates across all linked pages, whereas modifying HTML would require editing every single instance manually.
question: What happens if we disable CSS on a web page?
expectedAnswer: The content remains logically structured and readable due to HTML, but it loses all aesthetic layout, custom spacing, and colours, reverting to the browser's default settings.
activities.scaffolding: Definitions: 1. Content (Structure/Meaning): The information provided by HTML elements (headings, paragraphs, lists). 2. Presentation (Aesthetics/Layout): The visual appearance defined by CSS (colours, fonts, spacing, positioning).
activities.eLearning: https://www.stbrendans.qld.edu.au/
activities.transition: Transition students to the practical phase of applying CSS rules by linking an external stylesheet to their index.html document.

workbookSpec.title: Separation of Concerns Principles
workbookSpec.prompt: Fill in the blanks to define how HTML and CSS interact in web development.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: 1. structure, 2. presentation, 3. maintainability, 4. consistency
workbookSpec.text: The primary goal of modern web development is to ensure a strict separation between content and design. HTML serves as the document {{1}}, ensuring that the meaning and hierarchy of the page are defined clearly. Conversely, CSS manages the {{2}} layer, allowing developers to control aesthetics independently. By separating these two concerns, developers improve code {{3}}, as changes to design do not impact the raw data. Furthermore, using a single external stylesheet ensures visual {{4}} across multiple pages of a website.

activities.workbookMaterials: Guided notes worksheet: Separation of Concerns.
activities.teacherAnswerKey: 1. structure; 2. presentation; 3. maintainability; 4. consistency.

Navigate to the 'Computed' tab to reveal the Box Model visualizer. Point out: 'Note how the computed values differ from our CSS declaration due to browser defaults.' Model the relationship between the property (e.g., margin: 20px) and the visual orange highlight on screen.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher demonstration, then apply annotations to the provided diagram on the workbook sheet to map specific CSS properties to visual layout areas.
activities.visibleInstructions: Using the diagram provided, number the four layers of the Box Model from the centre outward. In the legend section, write the CSS property that controls the space within each layer.
activities.questioning:
question: If you increase the 'padding' property, which specific color band in the DevTools visualizer expands?
expected: The green band, as padding creates space inside the border, surrounding the content.
question: Why is it important to distinguish between 'margin' and 'padding' when positioning elements on the College website?
expected: Margin controls external spacing outside the border, while padding controls internal spacing within the element boundary; confusing them breaks alignment.
activities.scaffolding: The CSS Box Model represents every HTML element as a series of nested rectangular boxes: 1. Content (Innermost, where text/images sit), 2. Padding (Transparent area around content), 3. Border (The outline around padding), 4. Margin (Outermost space pushing elements away from others).
activities.eLearning: Use Browser Developer Tools (F12) to inspect the 'header' element on the St Brendan's College website and identify the computed margin, border, and padding values.
activities.transition: Transition to coding the box model properties by applying these values to your own class project stylesheet.

workbookSpec.title: The CSS Box Model Diagram

workbookSpec.figureHint: Include a cross-section diagram showing 4 nested concentric rectangles.

activities.workbookMaterials: Diagram of CSS Box Model (Nested layout blocks).
activities.teacherAnswerKey: Layer 1 (Innermost): Content - Controls the size of the text/image area. Layer 2: Padding - Controls space between content and border. Layer 3: Border - Controls the thickness/style of the perimeter. Layer 4 (Outermost): Margin - Controls space outside the element.

Using the 'Inspect' tool, model how adding padding expands the internal click area, whereas increasing margin pushes the button away from the browser edge or neighbouring elements. Provide the syntax pattern for the class selector.

activities.questioning:
question: If you increase padding, does the element grow larger or push other elements away?
expected: The element itself grows larger because padding is internal space.
question: How does the browser determine the total width of an element when padding and borders are added?
expected: The browser calculates total width as content width + padding + border (unless border-box is specified).

activities.title: Box Calculation Audit
activities.teacherDoes: Guide students through the 'Total Width' calculation using a worked example on the whiteboard. Write: 'Element: 100px width, 10px padding, 5px border'. Demonstrate: 100 + (2 * 10) + (2 * 5) = 130px. Emphasize that CSS box model calculations must account for both sides (left/right or top/bottom) of padding and borders.
activities.studentsDo: Calculate the total horizontal footprint of three CSS elements using the provided audit table. Apply the box model formula to determine how much space the element actually occupies on the screen.
activities.visibleInstructions: Audit the three provided elements. Calculate the total width using the standard box model formula. Write the final width in the 'Total' column for each case.
activities.questioning: 1. Why does the actual width on screen differ from the width property defined in CSS? Expected: Because the padding and borders are added to the specified width property by default (standard box-sizing). 2. How would adding 'box-sizing: border-box' change your calculation results? Expected: The padding and border would be included inside the defined width, changing the total to match the width property value.
activities.scaffolding: Formula: Width + (2 * padding) + (2 * border) = Total Width. Remember: padding and border values appear on both the left and right sides of an element.
activities.eLearning: Students access their CSS style sheets to identify existing padding and border values for current elements in their project.

activities.title: Linking Styles
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the syntax for external stylesheets: <link rel='stylesheet' href='style.css'>. Highlight that the href attribute is case-sensitive and must match the filename exactly. Model linking the stylesheet by typing it within the <head> section of a sample index.html. Emphasise that this single line of code enables consistent design across an entire website, adhering to the principle of separation of concerns.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the demonstration of external linking syntax. Open the provided workbook and complete the <link> tag within the <head> block to connect the stylesheet 'styles.css' to the index.html document.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the HTML link element in the editor below. Ensure the filename matches the 'styles.css' reference provided in the file directory.
activities.questioning:
question: Why is it more efficient to use an external CSS file instead of internal <style> tags within every HTML page?
expected: It allows for global updates to site appearance from a single file, ensuring consistency and reducing code repetition.
question: What happens if the href value in your link tag does not match the actual CSS filename?
expected: The browser will fail to locate the stylesheet, and the webpage will render without any of the intended custom styles.
activities.scaffolding: The <link> element must be placed inside the <head> of your document. Syntax required: <link rel="stylesheet" href="filename.css">

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Explicit instruction on how web browsers parse and interpret content; comparison of uncompressed assets against compressed versions; focus on technical impacts of file size on load times.

resources.value: Online compression tools, web performance testing tools, browser developer network logs, image editing software.

theory.value: Students investigate simple data compression techniques and their importance in web communication. Concepts such as file size, load time, and efficiency are explored. Students examine examples of compressed vs uncompressed data and discuss the impact on user experience.

prac.value: Students apply optimisation techniques to their webpages, such as resizing images and reducing file sizes. They compare performance differences between optimised and non-optimised files. Activities may include using online tools to compress images and analyse file sizes.

assessment.value: Formative: Checklist of code and asset optimization progress; students document the reduction in site load times.

lessons.title: Understanding Web Performance: The Cost of Bytes
lessons.learningGoal: Investigate how data compression techniques influence web communication efficiency and load times.

orientate.smartStart: Students view the homepages of St Brendan's College and Keppel Bay Marina. In 30 seconds, write down: which site loaded faster and why might there be a difference?
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can explain how file size impacts website load times and user experience

activities.title: Vocabulary: The Language of Performance
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly define 'Latency', 'Bandwidth', 'Compression', and 'Optimization'. Model the browser 'Network' tab (F12) to demonstrate how file sizes directly impact load times. Show an example of an unoptimized 5MB image vs a compressed 200KB version, noting that the browser must fully download the file before rendering. Script: 'Every kilobyte counts. When a webpage loads, it is essentially a conversation between your browser and a server; larger files make that conversation slower.'
activities.studentsDo: Identify and match the correct technical definitions for web performance metrics within their workbooks. Use the provided term bank to complete the definitions table.
activities.visibleInstructions: Use the term bank to match the correct definition to the performance vocabulary terms provided in the table.
activities.questioning:
question: Why does a larger image file increase load time?
expected: The browser must download more data packets from the server, increasing the total time required to complete the request over the network.
question: If a website has many unoptimized images, what happens to the user experience?
expected: The site will likely feel sluggish or unresponsive (high latency), which often leads to higher bounce rates as users become impatient.
activities.scaffolding: Definitions: Latency = The time interval between a request and the response; Bandwidth = The maximum capacity of a communication channel to transmit data; Compression = The process of encoding information using fewer bits than the original representation; Optimization = The process of modifying a system to make it work more efficiently or use fewer resources.
activities.eLearning: Teachers verify that all students can access browser Developer Tools (F12) and locate the 'Network' tab to observe asset loading.
activities.transition: We will now transition to analysing real-world local websites to identify these performance metrics in practice.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Latency: The time interval between a request and the response. Bandwidth: The maximum capacity of a communication channel to transmit data. Compression: The process of encoding information using fewer bits than the original representation. Optimization: The process of modifying a system to make it work more efficiently.

activities.title: Guided Notes: Browser Parsing
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate how a browser acts as a renderer, executing code sequentially. Using a live browser developer console, point out the 'waterfall' effect of loading assets. Explicitly differentiate between raw, uncompressed assets (high bandwidth) and optimized JPEGs (low bandwidth). Example: 'Notice how the server sends the HTML first, then the browser requests CSS and images. A 5MB image effectively pauses the page display, whereas a 200KB version loads instantly.'
activities.studentsDo: Complete the cloze passage in the workbook to reinforce the theoretical relationship between browser rendering and data compression.
activities.visibleInstructions: Fill in the missing terms in the paragraph below using the provided word bank to explain browser rendering processes.
activities.questioning:
question: What is the primary function of the browser when it encounters a large, unoptimized image file?
expected: The browser must download the entire file before it can fully render the surrounding layout, which blocks the critical rendering path.
question: Why does reducing file size through compression directly improve user experience?
expected: Smaller files require less time to transmit over a network, leading to faster content availability and reduced latency for the end user.
activities.scaffolding:
Browser Rendering Workflow:
1. Parsing: Browser reads the HTML structure.
2. Fetching: Browser identifies external resources (CSS, JS, Images).
3. Rendering: Browser draws content to the screen.
Compression Definition: The reduction of data size by removing redundant information without compromising the integrity of the file content.
activities.eLearning: Use Browser Developer Tools (Network Tab) to observe asset loading order.
activities.transition: Transitioning to the practical optimization task where students will manually resize assets.

lessons.title: Optimisation Techniques: Practical Application
lessons.learningGoal: Apply compression techniques to reduce image file sizes and improve webpage load times.

orientate.smartStart: View the provided list of file types (PNG, JPEG, SVG, GIF). Rank them by typical file size from smallest to largest.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can resize and compress images to optimize web performance

activities.title: I-Do: Compression Workflow
activities.teacherDoes: Model the full asset pipeline: select a high-resolution hero image (e.g., 5MB+), display the raw file properties, and run it through Squoosh or TinyPNG. Demonstrate the 'before/after' visual comparison slider. Narrate the decision-making process: 'We prioritize WebP or compressed JPEG for web assets to balance visual fidelity with site load performance. Notice how removing EXIF metadata and sub-sampling pixels provides the largest reduction in file size without perceptible loss to the human eye.' Provide a worked example of calculating compression percentage: (Original - New) / Original * 100.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the demonstration while completing the Compression Log. Record the file properties displayed on the projector to verify the reduction.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the teacher-led workflow. Record the original and optimized file sizes in your workbook. Calculate the percentage reduction for each asset processed.
activities.questioning:
question: How does the removal of non-visible metadata (EXIF) affect the file size compared to pixel-based compression?
expected: Removing metadata reduces file size instantly without affecting visual quality, whereas pixel-based compression actively changes image data, which can introduce artifacts.
question: In a real-world web environment for a business like Keppel Bay Marina, why is a 5MB image detrimental to user experience?
expected: Large files increase Time to First Byte (TTFB) and total page load time, frustrating mobile users on slower connections and negatively impacting search engine rankings.
question: What is the trade-off between aggressive 'lossy' compression and page performance?
expected: Aggressive lossy compression reduces file size significantly to improve speed, but results in 'pixelation' or blurring, which can damage the brand's professional aesthetic.
activities.scaffolding: Workflow Steps: 1. Identify raw image source. 2. Capture metadata (File Size/Dimensions). 3. Apply compression tool (WebP/JPEG). 4. Record output file size. 5. Calculate percentage reduction: [(Original - Compressed) / Original] × 100.
activities.eLearning: Teachers monitor rear-facing screens to ensure all students are viewing the performance metrics on the projector during the demonstration.
activities.transition: Transition students to independent practice using their own chosen web assets.

workbookSpec.title: Image Compression Analysis Log
workbookSpec.prompt: Document the compression process for your selected web assets. Analyse the impact of the compression algorithm on file efficiency.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Example Answer: 1. Baseline: 4.2MB, 1920x1080px. 2. Methodology: Conversion to WebP format, 75% quality setting. 3. Results: New size 420KB. Reduction: (4200KB - 420KB) / 4200KB = 90% reduction. The image is now 10x smaller, significantly improving browser load speed while maintaining visual clarity on desktop screens.

activities.title: We-Do: Comparative Analysis
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the workflow using a single, high-resolution sample image projected on screen. Model the process of checking metadata, utilizing a compression tool (such as TinyPNG or similar), and verifying the final byte size. Distribute the compression checklist. Facilitate a brief comparative discussion where students articulate why lossless vs. lossy compression impacts different image file types (e.g., JPEG vs. PNG) differently.
activities.studentsDo: Work in pairs to process the assigned high-resolution image through the optimization workflow. Document each step of the process on the physical checklist provided. Compare compression outcomes with a neighboring pair to identify variance in performance.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Open your assigned image file and record the original file size (in KB/MB). 2. Use the approved compression tool to reduce the file size without significant visual distortion. 3. Save the new version. 4. Verify that the new file size is lower than the original. 5. Complete the checklist.
activities.questioning:
question: If you reduce file size by 80% but the visual quality degrades significantly, is this a successful optimization? Why or why not?
expected: No, it is not successful. Optimization requires balancing file size reduction with acceptable user experience; if the image is pixelated, it fails the aesthetic requirements of the web project.
question: How do browsers process these compressed assets differently compared to raw, high-resolution files?
expected: Browsers download smaller files significantly faster, reducing the 'Time to First Meaningful Paint,' which directly improves user retention and page performance scores.
activities.scaffolding: Compression Workflow Criteria: 1. Asset selection (Format selection: JPEG for photos, PNG for graphics). 2. Metadata stripping (Removing EXIF data). 3. Resolution resizing (Matching dimensions to display requirements). 4. Quality vs. Size ratio (Finding the 'sweet spot').
activities.eLearning: Use Browser Developer Tools (Network Tab) to observe the 'Size' vs 'Transfer' metrics after uploading the optimized asset to the St Brendan's development server.
activities.transition: Transitioning to independent application, where students will apply these specific compression techniques to every asset on their assessment websites.

expected: Increased bounce rate due to slow load times on cellular networks, negatively impacting user experience and SEO rankings.
question: Why might you choose a lossy format like JPEG over a lossless format like PNG for a complex photograph?
expected: Lossy formats significantly reduce file size by discarding redundant pixel data that the human eye struggles to distinguish, whereas lossless formats maintain exact data integrity, leading to much larger file sizes.

lessons.title: Documenting Performance: The Final Audit
lessons.learningGoal: Evaluate and document the impact of asset optimization on total webpage load times.

orientate.smartStart: Quick Ranking: Place these actions in order of importance for web performance: (1) Minifying CSS, (2) Resizing images, (3) Changing font colors, (4) Compressing images.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can audit my project and explain the benefits of asset optimization

activities.title: I-Do: Auditing Workflow
activities.teacherDoes: Display the St Brendan's College mockup in a browser. Open Developer Tools (F12) and navigate to the Network tab. Demonstrate the 'Disable cache' toggle. Record the 'DOMContentLoaded' time for an unoptimized asset set. Replace the high-resolution images with optimized, compressed versions. Refresh the page and record the new load time. Explain: 'A 500KB image optimization reduces cumulative load, allowing the browser to render the DOM significantly faster.'
activities.studentsDo: Follow along on personal machines, navigating to the Network tab in the Chrome Developer Tools. Observe the demonstration of the impact of uncompressed files on the 'Finish' time indicator.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the teacher demonstration. Locate the Network tab in your browser's Developer Tools. Ensure the 'Disable cache' checkbox is checked during your audit.
activities.questioning: Why is 'Total Time' not always consistent across multiple refreshes? Expected: Network congestion, server load, and background background processes affect real-time speed. How does file size directly correlate to render-blocking resources? Expected: Large files take longer to download and parse, delaying the browser's ability to construct the DOM tree.
activities.scaffolding:
Audit Methodology: 
1. Open Network Tab (F12).
2. Filter by 'Img' or 'Media'.
3. Record 'Before' size.
4. Perform optimization (resize/compress).
5. Refresh and record 'After' size.
activities.eLearning: Use Chrome Developer Tools (Network Tab).
activities.transition: Proceed to conduct your own asset performance audit.

workbookSpec.title: Asset Performance Audit
workbookSpec.prompt: Document the performance metrics for your primary media assets before and after optimization.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Hero Banner Image: Expected reduction > 60%; Navigation Logo: Expected reduction > 40%; Footer Background: Expected reduction > 50%. Performance gain formula: ((Original - Optimized) / Original) * 100.

activities.title: We-Do: Peer Review
activities.teacherDoes: Model the constructive feedback process using a 'Think-Aloud' strategy. Display a sample (anonymised) audit table on the board. Say: 'When checking your partner's audit, look specifically at the difference between the 'Raw Size' and 'Compressed Size' columns. If the reduction is less than 20%, ask your partner if they applied a compression tool or simply resized the image dimension.' Provide students with a checklist for verification: 1. Are file extensions correct? 2. Is the math for percentage reduction accurate? 3. Does the suggested optimization method (e.g., JPEG compression, PNG to WebP) match the asset type?
activities.studentsDo: Exchange workbooks with a partner. Conduct a technical audit verification of their asset optimization documentation, checking calculations and the validity of their chosen optimization techniques. Write a specific, actionable piece of feedback for their improvement.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Exchange your audit documentation with a partner. 2. Verify their 'Pre-optimization' vs 'Post-optimization' file size calculations. 3. Check that the file compression method listed is appropriate for the asset type (e.g., WebP for images). 4. Write one specific suggestion for further improving their load times.
activities.questioning:
Did your partner identify any 'low hanging fruit' assets that offer the highest impact on load times? Expected: Students should identify large, uncompressed high-resolution images as the most impactful items for compression.
How does the 'Post-optimization' size differ from the raw file? Expected: It should demonstrate a measurable reduction in kilobytes, indicating successful application of compression algorithms or resizing.
activities.scaffolding: Peer Review Criteria: 1. Data Integrity: Audit figures accurately reflect file properties (KB/MB). 2. Logic: The optimization method (e.g., resizing vs. compressing) is suitable for the file type. 3. Actionability: Suggestion must specify 'What' (e.g., replace PNG with WebP) and 'Why' (e.g., lower file weight).
activities.eLearning: Use browser developer network logs to verify the partner's actual live asset sizes if discrepancies are found during peer audit.
activities.transition: Transition to the final documentation summary for the site audit report.

workbookSpec.title: Peer Audit Verification
workbookSpec.prompt: Evaluate your partner's documentation against the technical standards for performance optimization.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Teacher note: Ensure students are not just saying 'good job'. They must identify if a file format (e.g., PNG vs WebP) or compression setting is suboptimal.

sections.label: Peer Critique (Identify one specific optimization improvement)

activities.teacherAnswerKey: 1. Verification Checklist: Must confirm math (Raw - Optimized) / Raw * 100 = % saving. 2. Critique: Should identify specific miscalculations or suggest a more efficient format (e.g., 'Change this high-res PNG to a WebP format to reduce file size without losing visual fidelity'). 3. Recommendation: Must link the file size reduction directly to improved 'Time to First Byte' (TTFB) or overall page load speed.

activities.title: You-Do: Final Documentation
activities.teacherDoes: Teacher demonstrates how to capture the 'Network' tab log as evidence of improved load times. Teacher models the syntax for professional reflection: 'By reducing image resolution from 4K to 1080p, the asset file size decreased by 60%, resulting in a measurable reduction in page load latency, thus improving user experience.'
activities.studentsDo: Students export their optimized assets, verify file size reductions using the file properties, and complete the final audit documentation. Students link these performance metrics to user experience principles.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete your audit documentation. Justify your technical decisions regarding image compression, resolution, and file formats, referencing your recorded performance metrics.
activities.questioning:
question: How does the reduction of file size directly influence the 'Time to First Byte' (TTFB) or overall load performance?
expected: Smaller file sizes require less bandwidth and fewer data packets to be transferred from the server, resulting in faster rendering times for the client browser.
question: Why must a web developer document the 'before' and 'after' state of asset optimization?
expected: To provide empirical evidence of performance improvements, establish a baseline for future maintenance, and troubleshoot potential regressions in site speed.
activities.scaffolding:
Use the following terms in your justification: 
- Bandwidth: The transmission capacity of the connection. 
- Latency: The delay between a request and the response. 
- Compression (Lossy/Lossless): The reduction of data volume without significant loss of quality. 
- Optimization: The process of balancing quality against file size.
activities.eLearning: Review site metrics using the Browser Developer Tools (Network Tab) to compare load times before and after your asset optimization tasks.
activities.transition: Closing the lesson. Submit your final audit summary to the class submission folder.

workbookSpec.title: Asset Optimization Audit Log
workbookSpec.prompt: Evaluate the impact of your compression techniques on your final webpage performance.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Performance Metrics (Before & After): Must list specific file sizes (e.g., 'Before: 4.2MB, After: 450KB') and load times in milliseconds. Technical Justification: Must explain the trade-off between image fidelity and file size, citing the format chosen (e.g., WebP vs JPG) and why it was appropriate for the context. Impact on UX: Must link faster load times to higher retention rates and accessibility, particularly for mobile users on limited data connections.

culminate.smartFinish: Reflection: What was the biggest challenge in optimizing your files?

lessons.title: Revision: Web Architecture and Core Concepts
lessons.learningGoal: Define technical concepts related to web systems and architecture.

orientate.smartStart: Students complete a quick-fire matching quiz on the board: match the term (e.g., Client, Server, IP, DNS) to its fundamental role in web architecture.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can define technical concepts related to web systems and architecture

activities.title: Terminology Consolidation
activities.teacherDoes: Explain the client-server interaction model using the St Brendan's College homepage as a reference point. Demonstrate how a request travels from the browser, through DNS resolution, to the server, and returns the response. Emphasize the distinction between 'client-side' browser processing and 'server-side' data hosting.
activities.studentsDo: Identify and match the core technical components of web architecture in the provided terminology table.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Review the list of technical terms and their corresponding definitions in the bank. 2. Write the matching letter into the 'Match' column for each term.
activities.questioning:
question: What is the primary role of a server in the client-server model?
expected: To store, process, and transmit requested web resources and files back to the client application.
question: Why is DNS considered the 'phonebook of the internet'?
expected: Because it translates human-readable domain names (like www.stbrendans.qld.edu.au) into machine-readable IP addresses that computers use to locate each other.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions for Revision:
- Client: Software application (browser) requesting data from a server.
- Server: Host computer providing services or data to clients.
- DNS (Domain Name System): The naming system that links domain names to IP addresses.
- IP Address: Unique numerical identification label assigned to every device on a TCP/IP network.
activities.eLearning: Project the St Brendan's College home page (https://www.stbrendans.qld.edu.au/) to illustrate a live client-server interaction.
activities.transition: Transition to guided notes by summarising the dependency between DNS resolution and web resource loading.

workbookSpec.title: Web Architecture Matching
bank: A: Unique numerical label assigned to every device connected to a network.
B: Software/Hardware that provides data or services to other computers.
C: A software application used to enable a user to interact with the internet.
D: System that translates domain names into IP addresses.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Client: C, Server: B, DNS: D, IP Address: A

activities.title: Content, Structure, and Presentation
activities.teacherDoes: Distinguish between document structure and visual styling using the separation of concerns principle. Demonstrate this by loading the St Brendan's College homepage, disabling CSS in the browser inspector to reveal raw HTML structure, and then re-enabling it to show the visual presentation layer. Explicitly connect the concepts: 'HTML provides the semantic skeleton, while CSS acts as the aesthetic skin.' Provide a worked example of a tag pair (e.g., <header> vs <div>) to illustrate semantic relevance.
activities.studentsDo: Follow the teacher demonstration via their own device browsers (Developer Tools) to inspect page structure. Complete the cloze passage provided in the workbook to solidify terminology regarding web standards.
activities.visibleInstructions: Using your knowledge of web architecture, fill the blanks in the provided text. Refer to the word bank to ensure technical terms are applied correctly to the definitions of HTML and CSS.
activities.questioning:
question: What is the fundamental difference between HTML and CSS in the context of the client-server model?
Expected: HTML defines the logical structure and content of a document, whereas CSS dictates the presentation, layout, and visual formatting.
question: Why is the use of semantic tags like <article> or <nav> preferred over generic <div> tags?
Expected: Semantic tags provide machine-readable meaning to the browser and assistive technologies, improving accessibility and search engine optimisation (SEO) indexing.
activities.scaffolding: HTML: HyperText Markup Language. CSS: Cascading Style Sheets. Semantic Tags: HTML elements that clearly describe their meaning in a human- and machine-readable way (e.g., <header>, <footer>, <main>). Presentation: The visual appearance, including colours, fonts, and layout.
activities.eLearning: Use the browser's Developer Tools (F12) to inspect the St Brendan's College website structure. View the CSS 'Styles' pane to observe how rules affect rendering.
activities.transition: Transition to graphic mapping of system components and the client-server communication process.

workbookSpec.title: Web Architecture: Content and Style
workbookSpec.prompt: Complete the following summary regarding web standards.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: 1: HTML, 2: Structure, 3: CSS, 4: Presentation, 5: Browser
workbookSpec.text: The web relies on a separation of concerns to maintain efficient development. {{1}} acts as the backbone of a web document, defining the semantic {{2}} of the content by using specific tags rather than generic containers. Conversely, {{3}} is used to manage the visual {{4}} of the webpage. By keeping these layers separate, developers improve accessibility and maintainability. When the {{5}} parses these files, it combines the structure and the style rules to render the final page.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: 1: HTML | 2: Structure | 3: CSS | 4: Presentation | 5: Browser

activities.title: System Architecture Map
activities.teacherDoes: Display a simplified architectural diagram on the whiteboard. Model the flow: User Browser -> HTTP Request -> DNS Resolution (IP lookup) -> ISP/Infrastructure -> Web Server (Hosting Site) -> HTTP Response -> Browser Rendering. Emphasize that the 'Request' is the client asking for resources, while the 'Response' is the server returning data (HTML/CSS/JS).
activities.studentsDo: Complete the provided architectural map in the workbook, annotating the specific steps data takes when accessing a site like the St Brendan's College web page.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Label the diagram nodes: Client Browser, DNS Server, Internet (Cloud), and Hosting Server. 2. Draw arrows to indicate the bidirectional flow of the Request and Response. 3. Annotate the path with the term 'IP Address' where appropriate.
activities.questioning: If a user attempts to access a domain name that has not propagated through DNS servers, what is the result? Expected: The browser fails to resolve the URL to an IP address, resulting in a 'Server Not Found' or 'DNS Error'. What occurs if the request reaches the server, but the specific file requested (e.g., index.html) does not exist? Expected: The server returns a 404 Not Found status code within the response headers.
activities.scaffolding: Core components to include: [Client/Browser], [DNS Resolver], [Internet Backbone/Infrastructure], [Origin Server]. Request flow includes: URL input -> DNS Query -> IP Resolution -> HTTP GET Request -> Server Processing -> HTTP Response (200 OK).
activities.eLearning: View the 'St Brendan's College' official website to observe the final product of the request-response cycle: https://www.stbrendans.qld.edu.au/
activities.transition: Conclude the session with a summary check of the core revision concepts covered today.

workbookSpec.title: Request-Response Architecture Map
workbookSpec.prompt: Complete the diagram by labelling the nodes and drawing arrows representing the HTTP Request and HTTP Response paths.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Diagram should show a loop: Browser sends 'GET' arrow through DNS to Server. Server sends 'Response' arrow (HTML/Assets) back to Browser. Annotations include: Browser requests URL, DNS maps URL to IP, Server retrieves files, Browser renders content.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Diagram Order: [Browser] -> (sends GET Request) -> [DNS Resolver: translates URL to IP] -> [Internet Infrastructure: routing] -> [Web Server: processes request] -> (sends Response) -> [Browser: renders content]. Key annotations: Request contains headers and parameters; Response contains status codes (200, 404) and payload.

culminate.smartFinish: Peer-check: Students swap graphic maps and add one missing connection line.
culminate.summarise: Recap the three core concepts: Architecture, HTML/CSS separation, and Request/Response lifecycle.
culminate.nextSteps: Tomorrow: Practical exam question application.

lessons.title: Revision: Technical Application and Exam Practice
lessons.learningGoal: Construct appropriate technical justifications for exam responses.
